<reason>The debate narrowed to whether "legal responsibility" in the motion means fault attribution for the crash (CON) or any legally imposed duty triggered by rider-caused injuries (PRO). PRO won this because CON kept expanding what companies must legally do—a fare-funded injury surcharge paying the pedestrian, verified ID, app-deducted fines, mandatory suspensions, penalties for missed slowdowns—while insisting none of it counts. PRO's point that a fund which writes the victim's cheque is a duty to her, not merely "to the city," was not squarely answered, and PRO caught CON's drift from "committed no wrongful act" to conceding the omitted slowdown is "the company's own breach." CON landed real blows: the GPS-margin dilemma forced PRO to concede the fault presumption fires only in easy cases, and the causation/cheapest-cost-avoider framing was coherent. But CON's remaining route depends on a strained narrow reading of the motion, whereas PRO's reading (compulsory-insurance-style pay-first-then-recover, analogous to motor insurance) is natural and directly satisfied by CON's own remedies. PRO's two clipped turns are a minor execution cost but did not remove key content. Both sides used plausible general knowledge without fake precision.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B2.1–B2.2 ("Read CON's sixth paragraph again... That is the motion") turning CON's own surcharge into a concession, sustained through B5.1–B5.2, was decisive; CON's "regulatory duty to the city" reply (A4.1) failed because the fund pays the victim directly for a rider-caused injury.</best_rebuttal>
